newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania launches four-year privatisation plan.
newsitem.headline: Romania launches four-year privatisation plan.

text.p: Romania's new centrist government has launched a four-year programme to step up the languid pace of privatisation.
The programme spanning 1997-2000 promises to raise the private sector's stake of gross domestic product to around 80 percent from 52 percent last year.

"We have a programme envisaging privatisation targets, methods and strategies by sectors," Valentin Ionescu, president of the National Privatisation Agency (ANP), said during debates at the Romanian Economy Society.
Key targets under the plan -- a copy of which was made available to Reuters -- include lowering state intervention in the economy, attracting more foreign capital and boosting capital markets.

Privatisations, launched as a plank of market reforms after the 1989 fall of communism, have been mostly handled by the State Ownership Fund (FPS). Since its creation in 1992, the FPS managed to sell some 3,000 companies of the more than 6,500 enterprises in which it held 70 percent.
The leftist government which lost elections last year to a reformist coalition was repeatedly blamed for delaying selloffs, as were privatisation institutions for their lack of commitment to reforms.

The present government intends to reorganise the institutions, including the ANP and the FPS, to improve laws and solve payment arrears -- estimated at around 20 trillion lei ($2.85 billion) -- through debt-for-equity swaps.

The programme stipulates equity sale methods including public offers, worker-management buyouts and convertible bond issues, and ways to put company assets into private hands through cash sales and leasing.
In the shorter term, it gives priority to privatisation of banks and insurers to stimulate their role on the capital market.
As a step towards privatisation, the previous government launched a mass selloff in 1995 offering Romanians up to 60 percent in some 4,000 state companies in exchange for coupons.
Despite 90 percent subscription, economists did not call the scheme a success, saying the state still retained a controlling stake in the economy.

Lack of political commitment to reforms, financial bottlenecks, domestic capital shortages, unclear legislation and litigation over land ownership have often been cited as the reasons for fruitless privatisation.
